definitions.definition: DN 22:17-21 gives the four in short form (17) and then expands each: suffering (18), its origin (19), its cessation (20), the way (21).

DN 22:18: birth, ageing, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, despair, association with the disliked, separation from the liked, not getting what one wants are suffering; in brief the five aggregates of clinging are suffering. Also the narrow sense: bodily unpleasant feeling born of bodily contact.
DN 22:18: the being-born of beings in their various orders, coming to be, manifestation of the aggregates, acquisition of the sense bases.
DN 22:18: decrepitude, broken teeth, grey hair, wrinkled skin, decline of life-span, maturing of the faculties.
DN 22:18: the passing away and dissolution of beings from their order, the breaking up of the aggregates, the laying down of the body, the cutting off of the life faculty.
DN 22:18: sorrowing, grieving, inner sorrow in one struck by some misfortune or painful state.
DN 22:18: wailing and lamenting in one struck by some misfortune or painful state.
DN 22:18: mental pain, mental unpleasantness, unpleasant feeling born of mental contact.
DN 22:18: distress and despair in one struck by some misfortune or painful state.

DN 22:19: the craving that leads to renewed becoming, accompanied by delight and passion, delighting here and there; threefold: kāma-, bhava-, vibhava-taṇhā. It arises and settles wherever in the world there is the dear-looking and pleasant-looking (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind; their objects; consciousnesses; contacts; feelings; perceptions; volitions; cravings; thoughts; sustained thoughts). It is abandoned and ceases in the same places (dn22:20).
First of the three cravings (DN 22:19).
Second of the three cravings (DN 22:19).
Third of the three cravings (DN 22:19).

The 'places' where craving arises and takes root, and where it is abandoned and ceases (DN 22:19-20); the text lists the six sense bases, six objects, six consciousnesses, six contacts, six feelings, six perceptions, six volitions, six cravings, six thoughts and six sustained thoughts.
DN 22:20: the complete fading away and cessation (asesavirāganirodha) of that same craving, its giving up, relinquishment, release, non-reliance.
DN 22:21: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration, each defined in the sutta.
DN 22:21: knowledge of suffering, of its origin, of its cessation and of the way leading to its cessation.
DN 22:21: intention of renunciation (nekkhamma), of non-ill-will and of non-harming.
DN 22:21: abstaining from false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech and idle chatter.
DN 22:21: abstaining from killing living beings, from taking what is not given, and from sexual misconduct.
DN 22:21: the noble disciple abandons wrong livelihood and makes a living by right livelihood.

DN 22:21: generating desire, making effort, arousing energy, exerting the mind, striving for the non-arising of unarisen evil unwholesome states, the abandoning of arisen ones, the arising of unarisen wholesome states, and the persistence and fulfilment of arisen wholesome states.

DN 22:21: the monk abides contemplating body in body, feelings in feelings, mind in mind, dhammas in dhammas, ardent, clearly comprehending and mindful, having put away covetousness and displeasure for the world (that is, the four establishments of mindfulness).
DN 22:21: the four jhānas, each described.

DN 22:21 describes four as the content of right concentration: (1) secluded from sensual pleasures and unwholesome states, with thought and sustained thought, rapture and pleasure born of seclusion; (2) thought and sustained thought stilled, inner confidence, unification of mind, rapture and pleasure born of concentration; (3) rapture faded, equanimous, mindful, clearly comprehending, pleasure felt with the body; (4) pleasure and pain abandoned, neither painful nor pleasant, purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
